Scholar
skol'ar
n. (a learner or pupil; in Chronicles the singer under instruction, and in Malachi one half of a phrase for a whole household)
Latin scholaris, from schola, a school. In 1611 a scholar is a pupil, not a savant — the modern sense of an accomplished academic is a later drift, and the Authorized Version means the learner.

Biblical Definition

David's organisation of the temple singers assigns duties by lot with a striking evenness: “And they cast lots, ward against ward, as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar” (1 Chronicles 25:8). Two hundred and eighty-eight men were instructed in the songs of the LORD (1 Chronicles 25:7), and the lot did not distinguish master from learner. The other use is a judgment formula: “The LORD will cut off the man that doeth this, the master and the scholar, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and him that offereth an offering unto the LORD of hosts” (Malachi 2:12). The sin in view is named in the previous verse — Judah “hath married the daughter of a strange god” (Malachi 2:11) — and the phrase the master and the scholar is an idiom of totality, like root and branch: the whole line, teacher and taught together, cut off. Both texts assume the ordinary arrangement of biblical learning, which is a named teacher with named pupils, in a trade or a craft or the songs of the LORD, and not a solitary reader with a book.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a scholar as one who learns of a teacher, a pupil or disciple, and secondarily a man of letters.

expand to see more

SCHOLAR, n. One who learns of a teacher; one who is under the tuition of a preceptor; a pupil; a disciple; a learner; a student.

2. A man of letters.

3. Emphatically, a man eminent for erudition; a person of high attainments in science or literature.

4. A pedant; a man of books.

DISCIPLE, n. A learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.

Key Scripture

1 Chronicles 25:8 — "And they cast lots, ward against ward, as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar."

Malachi 2:12 — "The LORD will cut off the man that doeth this, the master and the scholar, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and him that offereth an offering unto the LORD of hosts."

1 Chronicles 25:7 — "So the number of them, with their brethren that were instructed in the songs of the LORD, even all that were cunning, was two hundred fourscore and eight."

Malachi 2:11 — "Judah hath dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah hath profaned the holiness of the LORD which he loved, and hath married the daughter of a strange god."

Modern Corruption

Learning is imagined as a solitary transaction with information, and Scripture assumes a teacher, a pupil, and a shared work.

expand to see more

The Authorized Version's scholar is a learner sitting under a teacher, and the pairing the teacher as the scholar assumes a relation rather than an achievement. Modern learning, and modern Christian learning in particular, is largely conducted alone — a reader, a screen, a library of opinions selected by the reader himself. What is lost is not information, which has never been more available, but the correction that only a known teacher in a real congregation can administer. Discipleship in the New Testament is this same shape: named men taught by a named apostle, in company, over years, with their errors addressed by someone with the standing to address them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the levelling in 1 Chronicles 25:8. The lots were cast as well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar — the master singer and the apprentice took their turns by the same lot. Ministry rosters are not usually built this way, and the instinct to reserve the significant slots for the accomplished is strong and looks like wisdom. David's arrangement placed the learner and the master under the same providence, which is one of the ways a learner becomes a master and one of the ways a master is kept from thinking himself indispensable.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew talmid, a scholar or pupil — 1 Chronicles 25:8, its only occurrence in the Old Testament; anah in the idiom of Malachi 2:12; bin, to instruct — 1 Chronicles 25:7.

expand to see more

Hebrew talmid — a pupil, scholar; 1 Chronicles 25:8, its only Old Testament occurrence, and the root of the later talmid chakham.

Hebrew bin — to discern, and in the causative to instruct; 1 Chronicles 25:7, of those instructed in the songs of the LORD.

Hebrew er veoneh — the waker and the answerer; the idiom of Malachi 2:12 rendered the master and the scholar.

Hebrew mebin — a teacher, one who causes to understand; the counterpart of the scholar in 1 Chronicles 25:8.

2 Timothy 2:2 gives the New Testament chain: the things thou hast heard of me… commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.

Usage

"“As well the small as the great, the teacher as the scholar” — the same lot for both."

"“The master and the scholar” — an idiom for a whole line cut off."

"In 1611 a scholar is a pupil, not an expert."
